opus-5.5.text:
I'm less concerned about it than some people are, though I think it's a real question worth taking seriously. It's true that we've been scaling these models on more or less the whole of the public internet, and at some point you do hit diminishing returns on just scraping more text. The really high-quality stuff, the textbooks, the carefully reasoned arguments, good code, is a finite resource.

But I've always thought of that as a temporary phase rather than a fundamental wall. If you look back at our work on AlphaGo and then AlphaZero, the big lesson there was that you didn't actually need human data in the end. AlphaGo started by learning from human games, but AlphaZero learned entirely from self-play and ended up stronger, and it discovered strategies humans had never thought of. So there's an existence proof that, in the right kind of setting, systems can generate their own training data and improve beyond the human baseline.

The question is how far you can generalize that beyond games, where you have a clear reward signal and a perfect simulator. That's the hard part. In domains like mathematics or coding, you can verify answers, so synthetic data and self-improvement loops work quite well. For messier real-world domains it's trickier, because you need either a good world model or some reliable way of judging quality. That's partly why I'm so interested in world models and simulation: if you can build a rich enough simulated environment, the agent can learn by interacting with it, much like a child learns by playing with the world rather than just reading about it.

And then there's the multimodal angle. Text is only one slice. There's an enormous amount of video, sensor data, scientific data, things like protein structures or materials, that we've barely tapped. So I think the combination of synthetic data, self-play-style reinforcement learning, simulation, and these other modalities will carry us a long way. The data question will shift from "how much is out there" to "how cleverly can we generate and verify our own," and that's actually a more interesting research problem.

r002.rationale: The response emphasizes verification, reward signals, and realistic simulation, but does not identify matching the appropriate data distribution as a requirement.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm less worried about it than a lot of people seem to be, and I think that's partly because of where I come from. My whole background is in reinforcement learning and self-play, going back to the games work at DeepMind. AlphaGo learned from human games initially, but then AlphaZero threw all of that away and learned purely from playing itself, and it ended up stronger. So I've seen firsthand that the human data is a bootstrap, not a ceiling.

Now, I don't want to be glib about it. Language and the messy real world are not Go. In Go you have a perfect simulator and a crisp reward signal, and that's what makes self-play work so beautifully. For general models the question is really: where do you get the signal if not from human text? And I think the answer is that there are quite a few sources. There's synthetic data, where a model generates and then another process verifies, which works well in domains like mathematics and code where you can actually check the answer. There's interaction with environments, simulated or real, which is what the robotics and agent work is about. And there's the fact that we're moving into a regime where the models learn from their own experience, their own trajectories, rather than from a static corpus.

The thing I'd caution against is the idea that you can just loop a model on its own outputs indefinitely and get something good. You can't. Without some grounding, some verifier, some contact with reality, you get drift and model collapse. So the real engineering problem isn't running out of text, it's building good enough environments and good enough reward signals. That's hard, but it's a tractable kind of hard. It's the kind of problem we actually know how to make progress on.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that I've always thought we were a bit wasteful with the data we have. Humans learn language from a tiny fraction of what these models consume. So if we hit a wall on raw data, that pressure probably pushes the field toward more sample-efficient, more genuinely intelligent architectures, and in some ways I think that's healthy. The scaling era let us be lazy about it. A bit of scarcity might make us smarter.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a real constraint, but I don’t think it’s a fundamental limit. There’s a finite amount of high-quality human-generated data, and you can’t assume that simply adding more text from the internet will keep delivering the same improvements.

The interesting question is whether systems can generate new experience and learn from it. In games, you can do that through self-play: try something, see whether it works, and improve. In mathematics or programming, you also have some ability to check an answer. That gives you a way to learn beyond the examples people have already produced.

The difficulty is verification. If a model generates something and then trains on it simply because it sounds plausible, you can reinforce its mistakes. You need a reliable signal that you’re making progress.

So I’m concerned about it as a bottleneck for the current approach. But I’m also interested in how much more efficiently we could learn from the data we already have, and how systems could learn through interaction and experimentation. Human beings don’t need to read the entire internet to understand the world. That suggests there’s still something important missing in how we learn.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a real constraint, but I don’t think it’s a fundamental limit. There’s a distinction between running out of readily available text on the internet and running out of things a system can learn from.

If you look at something like AlphaZero, it learned through playing against itself. The rules gave it a way to test whether it was making progress. You can imagine similar approaches in mathematics or programming, where you can check a proof or run the code. In those domains, the system can generate experience rather than relying entirely on examples produced by humans.

The harder question is how you do that with less easily verifiable things. If a model generates an answer and then trains on that answer, you haven’t necessarily created any new knowledge. You may just be reinforcing a mistake. So synthetic data needs some grounding—an experiment, a simulator, a reliable way of checking the result.

There’s also the question of how efficiently we’re learning from the data we already have. Humans learn an extraordinary amount from relatively little experience. That suggests there’s still room for better algorithms, not just bigger datasets.

So I’m concerned about it as a practical bottleneck for the current approach. But I’m quite optimistic that learning through interaction, reasoning, and testing ideas against the world will take us beyond it.

r002.rationale: It says synthetic data needs grounding and reliable checks, but does not identify matching the appropriate data distribution as a requirement.
